claim: YEATS2 is overexpressed in head and neck cancer (HNC).
source: YEATS2, that encodes for a histone reader protein, was the only gene that was significantly upregulated in cancer as compared to normal tissues (Figure 1C-D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data from 8 HNC tissue pairs (Figure 1C-D) and supplementary data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B).

claim: YEATS2 was upregulated in publicly available HNC microarray datasets GSE30784 and GSE9844.
source: YEATS2 was also found to be upregulated in publicly available HNC microarray datasets GSE30784 and GSE9844 (Figure 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by analysis of publicly available microarray datasets shown in Figure 1E-F.

claim: YEATS2 expression is significantly correlated with the expression of EMT-associated genes in TCGA data.
source: The association of YEATS2 with EMT was then established by a significant positive correlation observed between its expression and the expression of genes included in an EMT gene signature in TCGA data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: YEATS2 expression is upregulated in higher tumor grades (grades 2–4) compared to grade 1 tumors.
source: Moreover, the expression of YEATS2 was upregulated in higher tumor grades (grades 2–4) as compared to grade 1 tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA data stratified by tumor grade shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: YEATS2 expression is significantly correlated with the expression of metastasis-associated genes.
source: Additionally, on performing gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) using TCGA data, we found that YEATS2 expression is significantly correlated with the expression of metastasis-associated genes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: YEATS2 protein expression was increased in 23 head and neck cancer tissues compared to matched normal tissues.
source: On further investigation using immunoblotting, we found that the expression of YEATS2 protein was increased in a set of 23 head and neck cancer vs. matched normal tissues (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data from 23 HNC tissue pairs shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 1F.

claim: shRNA-mediated silencing of YEATS2 led to the downregulation of 2494 genes.
source: The shRNA-mediated silencing of YEATS2 led to the downregulation of 2494 genes, whereas 2073 genes were found to be upregulated (Figure 1H, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data in YEATS2-silenced BICR10 cells shown in Figure 1H and Supplementary file 2.

claim: EPITHELIAL MESENCHYMAL TRANSITION and OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION pathways were enriched among genes downregulated upon YEATS2 silencing.
source: Overrepresentation analysis revealed that hallmark gene sets from MSigDb (Molecular Signature Database) like OXIDATIVE PHOSPHORYLATION and EPITHELIAL MESENCHYMAL TRANSITION were some of the top pathways enriched among the downregulated genes (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by overrepresentation analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: YEATS2 knockdown decreases the expression of EMT markers Twist1, N-cadherin, and Vimentin in BICR10 and SCC9 cells.
source: we examined the expression of EMT markers in shControl vs. shYEATS2 BICR10 and SCC9 cells using immunoblotting and found that Twist1, N-cadherin, and Vimentin showed a decrease upon YEATS2 knockdown (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: YEATS2 downregulation significantly reduces the number of invading cells in Matrigel invasion assay.
source: Also, the number of invading cells significantly reduced in Matrigel invasion assay on YEATS2 downregulation, indicating that YEATS2 could be playing a role in the maintenance of EMT phenotype in HNC cells (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by Matrigel invasion assay data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: YEATS2 overexpression increases Twist1 expression and invasive capacity in BICR10 and SCC9 cells.
source: Conversely, the expression of Twist1 was increased and there was significant upregulation in invasive capacity of cells when BICR10 and SCC9 cells were transfected with YEATS2-overexpression construct (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting and invasion assay data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: YEATS2-silenced cells migrate slower than control cells in wound healing assay.
source: Wound healing assay was performed to assess the cell migration property of HNC cells and it was found that YEATS2-silenced cells migrated slower than control cells (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: YEATS2 overexpression results in faster wound healing compared to control cells.
source: On the other hand, overexpressing YEATS2 in BICR10 and SCC9 cells resulted in faster wound healing as compared to control cells (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by wound healing assay data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: YEATS2 downregulation reduces the ability of tumor spheres to invade a collagen matrix in 3D invasion assay.
source: It was observed that a reduced number of cells invaded the collagen matrix when YEATS2 was downregulated. The opposite pattern was observed in both the cell lines when YEATS2 was overexpressed (Figure 2F–G, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: Supported by 3D invasion assay data shown in Figure 2F–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–H.

claim: SP1 is directly responsible for YEATS2 upregulation in HNC.
source: These results indicate that SP1 is directly responsible for YEATS2 upregulation in HNC.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assays, ChIP-qPCR, and site-directed mutagenesis experiments showing SP1 binding to YEATS2 promoter and regulating its expression.

claim: A significant decrease in luciferase activity was observed for the shorter YEATS2 promoter-deletion construct (Luc-311) compared to the full-length construct (Luc-508).
source: A significant decrease in the luciferase activity was observed for shorter promoter-deletion construct (Luc-311) compared to the full-length construct (Luc-508) (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SP1 was significantly upregulated in tumor vs. normal patient data in TCGA mRNA expression dataset for HNC.
source: Expression profiles of these transcription factors in the TCGA mRNA expression dataset for HNC showed that unlike KLF5, SP1 was significantly upregulated in tumor vs. normal patient data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: shRNA-mediated silencing of SP1 led to decreased expression of YEATS2 in HNC cell lines.
source: Furthermore, shRNA-mediated silencing of SP1 led to decreased expression of YEATS2 in the HNC cell lines (Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3B–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: SP1 shows significant enrichment on YEATS2 promoter in ChIP assay.
source: Furthermore, on performing SP1-ChIP assay, we found significant enrichment of SP1 on YEATS2 promoter when compared with control IP in both the cell lines (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by SP1-ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Luciferase activity decreased in SP1-knockdown condition using Luc-508 construct.
source: Next, we also performed luciferase assay using Luc-508 construct in SP1-knockdown condition, and found a decreased luciferase activity as compared to control (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Mutation of SP1 consensus binding sites in YEATS2 promoter construct resulted in nearly 50% decrease in luciferase activity.
source: After performing luciferase assay, nearly 50% decrease in luciferase activity was observed for the mutant promoter construct, compared to its wild-type counterpart (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by luciferase assay data with mutant construct shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Ectopic expression of YEATS2 in shSP1 cells partially rescues Twist1 expression.
source: We then checked the status of invasion in shSP1 cells and found that the EMT-marker Twist1 was reduced in these cells. However, the ectopic expression of YEATS2 in shSP1 cells was able to rescue Twist1 expression partially (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: YEATS2 overexpression rescues the decrease in invasion observed in shSP1 cells.
source: We then performed an invasion assay to check the effect of YEATS2 overexpression in the background of SP1-knockdown, and found that there was a decrease in invasion in shSP1 cells, which was rescued by overexpression of YEATS2 (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1H.

claim: KEGG LYSINE DEGRADATION was the top-most pathway associated with high YEATS2 expression in TCGA samples.
source: For this, we performed gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) with a comprehensive list of essential metabolic pathways (Su et al., 2020) and found out that KEGG LYSINE DEGRADATION was the top-most pathway associated with high YEATS2 expression in TCGA samples (Figure 4A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 4A and Supplementary file 3, with citation to Su et al., 2020.

claim: YEATS2 has a higher affinity for binding crotonyl groups on histone (specifically on H3K27 residue) than other histone substrates.
source: Since it is known that YEATS2 has a higher affinity for binding crotonyl groups on histone (specifically on H3K27 residue) than other histone substrates (Zhao et al., 2016), we hypothesized that the crotonyl-CoA producing enzyme glutaryl CoA dehydrogenase (GCDH), which is a part of lysine degradation pathway, would have increased expression in HNC.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2016.

claim: GCDH was upregulated in TCGA cancer vs. normal tissue dataset.
source: We found that GCDH was upregulated and had an inverse pattern of expression with the downstream enzyme ECHS1 (Enoyl Coenzyme A hydratase, short chain 1) in TCGA cancer vs. normal tissue dataset (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: ECHS1 had an inverse pattern of expression with GCDH in TCGA cancer vs. normal tissue dataset.
source: We found that GCDH was upregulated and had an inverse pattern of expression with the downstream enzyme ECHS1 (Enoyl Coenzyme A hydratase, short chain 1) in TCGA cancer vs. normal tissue dataset (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: GCDH mRNA expression was significantly upregulated in head and neck cancer samples relative to their matched normal tissues.
source: Furthermore, we found that the mRNA expression of GCDH was significantly upregulated in head and neck cancer samples relative to their matched normal tissues (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GCDH and YEATS2 expression levels show significant Spearman correlation coefficient value of 0.32 in TCGA data.
source: Moreover, correlation analysis performed between the expression levels of GCDH and YEATS2 in TCGA data showed significant Spearman correlation coefficient value of 0.32 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The abundance of H3K27cr histone mark was higher in tumor compared to normal in HNC tissues.
source: We then proceeded to check the levels of histone crotonylation (H3K27cr) in a set of nuclear protein lysates obtained from HNC tissues and found that the abundance of this histone mark was higher in tumor as compared to normal (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ECHS1 expression was notably reduced in tumor tissues compared to adjacent normal tissues by IHC.
source: ECHS1 expression was notably reduced in tumor tissues, whereas GCDH, YEATS2, H3K27cr, and Twist1 exhibited increased staining intensity in tumor sections compared to the adjacent normal tissues (Figure 4E–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4E–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: GCDH, YEATS2, H3K27cr, and Twist1 exhibited increased staining intensity in tumor sections compared to the adjacent normal tissues by IHC.
source: ECHS1 expression was notably reduced in tumor tissues, whereas GCDH, YEATS2, H3K27cr, and Twist1 exhibited increased staining intensity in tumor sections compared to the adjacent normal tissues (Figure 4E–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4E–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nuclear GCDH was detected in HNC tissues by immunohistochemistry.
source: Using immunohistochemistry, we detected the presence of nuclear GCDH in HNC tissues and observed that the regions that stained strongly for nuclear GCDH, also showed abundance in H3K27cr (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Regions that stained strongly for nuclear GCDH also showed abundance in H3K27cr.
source: Using immunohistochemistry, we detected the presence of nuclear GCDH in HNC tissues and observed that the regions that stained strongly for nuclear GCDH, also showed abundance in H3K27cr (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: YEATS2 knockdown causes a decrease in H3K27cr levels.
source: Further, on checking the levels of H3K27cr on YEATS2- and GCDH-knockdown using immunoblotting and immunofluorescence, we found that the cells silenced for either of the two genes caused a decrease in H3K27cr levels (Figure 4G–J, Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G–J and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–B.

claim: GCDH knockdown causes a decrease in H3K27cr levels.
source: Further, on checking the levels of H3K27cr on YEATS2- and GCDH-knockdown using immunoblotting and immunofluorescence, we found that the cells silenced for either of the two genes caused a decrease in H3K27cr levels (Figure 4G–J, Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4G–J and Figure 4—figure supplement 4A–B.

claim: YEATS2 overexpression increases H3K27cr signal.
source: On the other hand, an increase in H3K27cr signal was observed when YEATS2 was overexpressed ectopically in BICR10 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4C.

claim: SPARC was the common gene present in YEATS2 ChIP-seq peaks on promoters, genes downregulated in shYEATS2 RNA-seq, and hallmark EMT gene signature.
source: We then performed integration of those genes having YEATS2 ChIP-seq peaks on their promoters with the genes that were downregulated in shYEATS2 vs. shControl RNA-seq data, and the genes included in the hallmark EMT gene signature. We found that SPARC was the common gene present in all 3 sets (Figure 5A-B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by integration of ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, and EMT gene signature data shown in Figure 5A-B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: SPARC mRNA expression level in TCGA dataset was higher in tumor compared to normal.
source: The mRNA expression level of SPARC in TCGA dataset was also found to be higher in tumor as compared to normal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: YEATS2 binding on SPARC promoter decreased on YEATS2 knockdown in BICR10 and SCC9.
source: By performing YEATS2 ChIP-qPCR in YEATS2-downregulated cells, we found that the binding of YEATS2 on SPARC promoter decreased on its knockdown in BICR10 as well as SCC9 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by YEATS2 ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: SPARC expression decreased in YEATS2-knockdown conditions in both BICR10 and SCC9 cell lines.
source: We then checked the expression of SPARC at the RNA level on YEATS2-downregulation. SPARC expression was decreased in YEATS2-knockdown conditions in both the cell lines (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Secreted SPARC levels decreased in conditioned media from shYEATS2 BICR10 cells.
source: Since SPARC is a secretory protein, we investigated its level in conditioned media obtained from shControl and shYEATS2 BICR10 cells. We found a decrease in the secreted pool of SPARC on YEATS2-knockdown (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting of conditioned media shown in Figure 5E.

claim: p300 (EP300 gene) had increased expression in tumor vs. normal HNC dataset.
source: For this, we checked the expression of p300, a known writer of H3K27cr mark (Xie et al., 2024a) in humans, in TCGA dataset. We found that p300 (EP300 gene) had increased expression in tumor vs. normal HNC dataset (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G, with citation to Xie et al., 2024a.

claim: p300 binding on SPARC promoter was reduced in YEATS2-silenced BICR10 cells.
source: On performing p300-ChIP assay, it was found that its binding was reduced in YEATS2-silenced BICR10 cells when compared to the shControl cells, indicating the potential role of p300 in leading to increased expression of SPARC in HNC cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by p300-ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SPARC expression in supernatant derived from shEP300 BICR10 cells was reduced compared to shControl cells.
source: To validate our claim, we performed immunoblotting after p300 knockdown and found that the expression of SPARC in supernatant derived from shEP300 BICR10 cells was reduced as compared to shControl cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: YEATS2 and p300 function together as a complex.
source: Furthermore, we performed p300 pulldown in a co-immunoprecipitation experiment to check if YEATS2 and p300 function in a protein complex. We discovered the presence of YEATS2 in the p300-immunoprecipitate sample, clearly indicating that YEATS2 and p300 function together as a complex to drive the expression of SPARC (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: SPARC overexpression rescues the decrease in invasion seen on YEATS2-downregulation.
source: Finally, we wanted to check the effect of SPARC on invasion. It was observed that the decrease in invasion seen on YEATS2-downregulation was rescued by SPARC overexpression (Figure 5I–J).
evidence: Supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 5I–J.

claim: SPARC is a direct target of YEATS2 and acts as a downstream effector of YEATS2 in maintaining invasive phenotype in HNC cells.
source: This indicates that SPARC is a direct target of YEATS2 and acts as a downstream effector of YEATS2 in maintaining invasive phenotype in HNC cells.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments showing SPARC overexpression restores invasion in YEATS2-knockdown cells.

claim: Only H3K27cr mark showed significant downregulation on YEATS2 knockdown at the SPARC promoter, not H3K27ac.
source: We performed ChIP-qPCR assay to check the abundance of both the marks at the SPARC promoter and found that only H3K27cr mark showed significant downregulation on YEATS2 knockdown (Figure 6A–B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6A–B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: RNA Pol II occupancy on SPARC promoter decreased after YEATS2 knockdown.
source: Furthermore, to validate the role of YEATS2 in the transcription of SPARC gene, we performed RNA Pol II ChIP-qPCR assay and observed a decrease in Pol II occupancy on SPARC promoter after YEATS2 knockdown (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by RNA Pol II ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Sodium crotonate treatment increased H3K27cr levels on SPARC promoter.
source: Since the substrate used in addition of crotonylation marks on histones is crotonyl-CoA, we supplemented the cells with its precursor molecule sodium crotonate (Sabari et al., 2015), and saw that there was an increase in H3K27cr levels on SPARC promoter (Figure 6D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, with citation to Sabari et al., 2015.

claim: Sodium crotonate treatment increased SPARC expression at mRNA and protein levels in both BICR10 and SCC9 cell lines.
source: We also observed an increase in the expression of SPARC at mRNA and protein levels in both the cell lines (Figure 6E–F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6E–F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: Cells treated with crotonate invaded in greater numbers in Matrigel than untreated cells in both HNC cell lines.
source: We then checked the effect of crotonate on cancer cell invasiveness and observed that cells treated with crotonate invaded in greater numbers in Matrigel than untreated cells in both the HNC cell lines (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Crotonate treatment did not significantly rescue H3K27cr levels on SPARC or SPARC protein expression in YEATS2-downregulated cells.
source: Finally, we checked whether crotonate treatment can rescue the effect of YEATS2 downregulation on SPARC expression. We did not observe significant rescue either in H3K27cr levels on SPARC or in SPARC protein expression, when YEATS2-downregulated cells treated with crotonate (Figure 6H–I).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 6H–I.

claim: H3K27cr-mediated increase in SPARC expression is subject to the availability of YEATS2 in HNC cells.
source: With these observations, we can conclude that H3K27cr-mediated increase in SPARC expression is subject to the availability of YEATS2 in HNC cells.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that crotonate cannot rescue SPARC expression in YEATS2-knockdown cells.

claim: p300 knockdown led to a significant decrease in H3K27cr levels on SPARC promoter.
source: For this, we performed p300 knockdown followed by H3K27cr-ChIP-qPCR and found a significant decrease in H3K27cr levels on SPARC promoter in shEP300 BICR10 cells (Figure 6J).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6J.

claim: p300 regulates SPARC expression by functioning as a crotonyltransferase.
source: This indicates that p300 regulates SPARC expression by functioning as a crotonyltransferase.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that p300 knockdown decreases H3K27cr levels on SPARC promoter.

claim: p300 occupancy on SPARC decreased in SP1 knockdown cells and was rescued by overexpressing YEATS2.
source: As expected, on performing p300-ChIP-qPCR we saw a decrease in p300 occupancy on SPARC in SP1 knockdown cells, which was rescued by overexpressing YEATS2 in shSP1 cells (Figure 6K).
evidence: Supported by p300-ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: H3K27cr enrichment on SPARC promoter decreased in shSP1 cells and was rescued by YEATS2 overexpression.
source: We observed the same pattern in the H3K27cr levels—decreased enrichment of H3K27cr in shSP1 cells and its subsequent rescue on YEATS2 overexpression (Figure 6L).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6L.

claim: The expression of EMT-related gene SPARC is regulated by promoter H3K27cr levels added by crotonyltransferase p300, whose recruitment is dependent on the histone reader YEATS2.
source: In conclusion, the expression of EMT-related gene SPARC is regulated by promoter H3K27cr levels added by crotonyltransferase p300, whose recruitment is dependent on the histone reader YEATS2.
evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing YEATS2 recruits p300, which adds H3K27cr marks to regulate SPARC expression.

claim: GCDH knockdown led to a decrease in SPARC at protein and mRNA levels.
source: On performing knockdown of GCDH, we observed a decrease in SPARC at protein and mRNA levels (Figure 7A–B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7A–B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3K27cr marks on SPARC promoter reduced in GCDH-downregulated cells.
source: Also, on performing H3K27cr-ChIP assay with GCDH-downregulated cells, we found that H3K27cr marks on SPARC promoter reduced relative to control cells (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: GCDH and YEATS2 do not directly interact.
source: We then sought to explore the possibility of localized histone crotonylation performed by a multi-protein complex consisting of YEATS2 and GCDH. For this, we performed co-immunoprecipitation; however, we did not observe an interaction between GCDH and YEATS2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B), ruling out the possibility of the localized production of crotonyl-CoA at a specific gene locus (Kinnaird et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B, with citation to Kinnaird et al., 2016.

claim: TCGA gene expression dataset showed a significant correlation between the expression levels of SP1 and GCDH.
source: We then checked whether both the genes are regulated by the same transcription factor i.e., SP1. TCGA gene expression dataset showed a significant correlation between the expression levels of SP1 and GCDH, hinting at the possibility of SP1 transcriptionally regulating GCDH in HNC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SP1 knockdown led to a decrease in GCDH levels in both HNC cell lines.
source: Thus, we performed SP1-knockdown and found a decrease in GCDH levels in both HNC cell lines (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1D.

claim: SP1 shows significant occupancy on GCDH promoter in BICR10 and SCC9.
source: On performing SP1-ChIP we found a significant occupancy of SP1 on GCDH promoter in BICR10 and SCC9 (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by SP1-ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1E.

claim: SP1 is responsible for high expression of both GCDH and YEATS2 in HNC.
source: These results suggest that SP1 is responsible for high expression of both GCDH and YEATS2 in HNC.
evidence: Inferred from experiments showing SP1 binds to and regulates both GCDH and YEATS2 promoters.

claim: GCDH downregulation led to a significant decrease in the invasive capacity of BICR10 cells.
source: We performed a Matrigel invasion assay with shControl and shGCDH BICR10 cells and found a significant decrease in the invasive capacity of shGCDH cells (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: GCDH overexpression increased the number of invading BICR10 cells.
source: Conversely, the number of invading cells showed an increase when GCDH was overexpressed in BICR10 cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1F), indicating that like YEATS2, GCDH is also essential for imparting invasive properties to HNC cells.
evidence: Supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Nuclear localization of GCDH diminished in shYEATS2 cells compared to shControl cells.
source: We detected the presence of GCDH in nucleus in BICR10 using IF, and observed that the levels of nuclear GCDH diminished in shYEATS2 cells as compared to shControl cells (Figure 7G).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: YEATS2 might be involved in regulating the transport of GCDH inside nucleus indirectly by an unknown mechanism.
source: This indicates that YEATS2 might be involved in regulating the transport of GCDH inside nucleus indirectly by an unknown mechanism.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that nuclear GCDH levels decrease in YEATS2-knockdown cells.

claim: Dual overexpression of YEATS2 and GCDH in SP1-silenced cells rescued SPARC levels to a greater degree than individual overexpression.
source: The dual overexpression of YEATS2 and GCDH in SP1-silenced cells rescued the SPARC levels to a greater degree; whereas, YEATS2 and GCDH when overexpressed alone, could only partially rescue SPARC expression (Figure 7H).
evidence: Supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: One of the axes involved in regulation of EMT in HNC is dependent on the synergistic maintenance of H3K27cr marks on SPARC gene by YEATS2 and GCDH.
source: Hereby, we establish that one of the axes involved in regulation of EMT in HNC is dependent on the synergistic maintenance of H3K27cr marks on SPARC gene by YEATS2 and GCDH.
evidence: Inferred from rescue experiments showing synergistic effect of YEATS2 and GCDH on SPARC expression.

claim: Downregulation of YEATS2 led to a significant change in H3K27cr enrichment at 1583 locations in the genome, with 1533 locations showing a significant decrease.
source: We found that downregulation of YEATS2 led to a significant change in H3K27cr enrichment at 1583 locations in the genome, out of which 1533 locations showed a significant decrease in H3K27cr enrichment (Figure 8A).
evidence: Supported by H3K27cr ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: 1166 differentially lost H3K27cr sites were found to be present at the promoter regions of genes.
source: Further, 1166 differentially lost sites were found to be present at the promoter regions of genes.
evidence: Stated as a result from H3K27cr ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: EPITHELIAL MESENCHYMAL TRANSITION was one of the enriched hallmark gene sets among genes with reduced H3K27cr levels.
source: As expected, overrepresentation analysis using these set of genes revealed EPITHELIAL MESENCHYMAL TRANSITION as one of the enriched hallmark gene sets (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by overrepresentation analysis shown in Figure 8B.

claim: 147 genes were found to be common in both genes with reduced H3K27cr levels and genes downregulated in shControl vs. shYEATS2 RNA-seq.
source: We then overlapped the genes having reduced H3K27cr levels with the genes that showed downregulation in shControl vs. shYEATS2 RNA-seq. A total of 147 genes were found to be common in both the sets (Figure 8C, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by integration of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 8C and Supplementary file 5.

claim: ERG and CREB3L2 are examples of EMT-associated genes among the 147 genes common in both reduced H3K27cr and downregulated RNA-seq sets.
source: Among these 147 genes, some examples of EMT-associated genes were ERG (Leshem et al., 2011) and CREB3L2 (Yuxiong et al., 2023; Figure 8D–E).
evidence: Supported by IGV plots shown in Figure 8D–E, with citations to Leshem et al., 2011 and Yuxiong et al., 2023.

claim: YEATS2 regulates histone crotonylation throughout the genome resulting in the transcriptional activation of a large number of genes, many of which are related to the process of EMT.
source: Overall, our results suggest that YEATS2 regulates histone crotonylation throughout the genome resulting in the transcriptional activation of a large number of genes, many of which are related to the process of EMT.
evidence: Inferred from H3K27cr ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data showing global effects of YEATS2 on histone crotonylation and gene expression.

claim: The YEATS domain confers unique properties to YEATS2, making it suitable for binding with modifications other than acetylation.
source: The YEATS domain confers unique properties to this epigenetic factor, making it suitable for binding with modifications other than acetylation (Zhao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2017.

claim: YEATS2 had the highest affinity for histone crotonylation, specifically at the histone H3 lysine 27 position.
source: Among all histone modifications screened, YEATS2 had the highest affinity for histone crotonylation, specifically at the histone H3 lysine 27 position (Zhao et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2016.

claim: High H3K27cr at the promoter of ETS1 gene led to an increase in its expression and promoted metastasis in colorectal cancer.
source: Conversely, another study in colorectal cancer showed that high H3K27cr at the promoter of ETS1 gene led to an increase in its expression and promoted metastasis (Liao et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liao et al., 2023.

claim: SPARC mediates ECM-tumor cell communication as a part of the tumor microenvironment.
source: As a part of the tumor microenvironment, SPARC mediates ECM-tumor cell communication. Several reports have suggested the role of SPARC in contributing towards a pro-invasive phenotype in cells of multiple cancer types (Carriere et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carriere et al., 2021.

claim: Presence of SPARC in tumor stroma was reported to be responsible for recruitment of immunosuppressive myeloid cells in high-grade breast carcinomas.
source: Presence of SPARC in tumor stroma was reported to be responsible for recruitment of immunosuppressive myeloid cells in high-grade breast carcinomas (Sangaletti et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sangaletti et al., 2016.

claim: p300-mediated crotonylation at H3K27 and other histone residues is important in early embryonic development.
source: Recent studies have highlighted the importance of p300-mediated crotonylation at H3K27 and other histone residues in the crucial process of early embryonic development. Depletion of p300 led to reduced histone crotonylation resulting in dysregulated gene expression in developing embryos causing them to be arrested at the 8 cell stage (Gao et al., 2024).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gao et al., 2024.

claim: Epigenetic changes and aberrant metabolism are both major hallmarks of cancer.
source: Since epigenetic changes and aberrant metabolism are both major hallmarks of cancer (Diehl and Muir, 2020; Li et al., 2018), it is important to investigate the metabolism-epigenetics axis in order to yield new therapeutic targets.
evidence: Supported by citations to Diehl and Muir, 2020 and Li et al., 2018.

claim: The upregulation of both YEATS2 and GCDH contributes towards the enhancement of EMT in head and neck cancer by changes in the global EMT-favoring gene expression, mediated through promoter histone crotonylation.
source: In conclusion, we have presented a sophisticated interplay between YEATS2 and GCDH, where the upregulation of both factors contributes towards the enhancement of EMT in head and neck cancer by changes in the global EMT-favoring gene expression, mediated through promoter histone crotonylation (Figure 9).
evidence: Inferred from the collective experimental data presented in the study, summarized in Figure 9.

claim: The YEATS2–GCDH–SPARC axis is a potential therapeutic target in HNC.
source: Our findings provide new insights into the metabolic–epigenetic crosstalk driving EMT and identify the YEATS2–GCDH–SPARC axis as a potential therapeutic target in HNC.
evidence: Inferred from the study's findings showing the importance of this axis in HNC progression.
